newsitem.title: USA: Florida gives red light to beach driving.
newsitem.headline: Florida gives red light to beach driving.

text.p: Beach driving, once common throughout Florida, may be losing its last foothold -- Daytona Beach, a city built on the twin images of automobiles and surfside fun.

As soon as Volusia County's government can come up with 1,000 new parking spaces, driving along the most historic and popular stretch of an area known since the 1920s as "The World's Most Famous Beach" will come to an end, officials said on Friday.

"We can't cling to a dying tradition so long that we lose the public," said Jon Kaney, a local attoney who has worked with developers and hotel owners to end the beach driving. "Those were the days, but they're not the future. That's the past."

At issue is a single mile of beach declared off-limits by the county council on Thursday. Beach driving will still be permitted in some other areas, but beach-driving advocates say it is the beginning of the end.

"Once the hotels start making money, everyone else with beachfront property will want to make a buck, too," said Joe Pierson, who drives his 1961 Corvair along the beach nearly every day. "This was the last city beach in Florida that belonged to the people and not the developers."

Daytona Beach has an unusually hard, wide beach that became popular with drivers at the turn of the century. Tycoons like William K. Vanderbilt and Ransom Olds, who created the Oldsmobile, used to race early-model automobiles on the beach and established the world's first official land speed records.

Later, in the 1920s, an English army officer, Henry Segrave, came to the beach and was the first man to drive 200 mph, using a car powered by aircraft engines designed for the Royal Air Force. King George V knighted him for his accomplishment.

For years new speed records were set each year along Daytona Beach. And in the 1930s and 1940s the racing body that would eventually become NASCAR began stock car racing on the sands before building the Daytona International Speedway.

The problem today, says the anti-auto crowd, is that the same budget motels that appealed to tourists in the middle of the century are still there, but the families have mostly gone to Disney World in Orlando.

"When you drive down state road A-1A and see hotels with signs that advertise clean rooms, you've got a problem," said Lynne Plaskett, a county council member who joined the unanimous vote to end the driving. "We've had a bad image for so long."
But the loss is being felt deeply by others. "The beach and the driving is Daytona Beach," said Jim Tyler, a native. "For some of us, it is a lot more important than having big new hotels."
